title: Lalla of Kashmir
hookLine: a knot for every insult, a knot for every compliment, and at night two cloths that weigh the same
tomorrow: her teacher gave Lalla only one teaching. what was it?

cards: At the reception, Theo got two reviews in ten minutes. One aunt hugged him and called him a blessing. Another, over the cake, called him the lost sheep.
He's been replaying both all night. Here's a strange old story for him. A wandering woman in Kashmir asks a cloth seller to cut a cloth into two equal pieces, and she lays one over each shoulder.
All day, when someone mocks her, she ties a knot in one. When someone praises her, a knot in the other. At evening she has the merchant weigh them.

teach.b: The woman is Lalla, a yogini devoted to Shiva, and her sayings, called vakhs, are short poems in Kashmiri. The story is a legend, told about her in Kashmir, but it solves its own puzzle.
Of course the cloths weigh the same: the knots are just knots. The praise didn't add anything to her, and the insults didn't take anything away.
That's what the knots were for: to show the merchant, and anyone watching, that both kinds of words had landed on cloth, not on her. Lalla says it in one of her own vakhs, too.

teach.h: LET THEM JEER; LET THEM BRING FLOWERS.
teach.b: Let them abuse me or jeer at me, let them worship me with flowers; I gain nothing from any of it, and I stay as I am. Here's the teaching behind it.

Lalla belonged to Kashmir's Shaiva tradition, which teaches that Shiva is the true Self of every being. If that's who you are underneath, then a compliment can't make you more, and a cruel word can't make you less.
One more thing about her: Hindus and Muslims in Kashmir both claim her, and both still quote her vakhs. So for Theo: both aunts' words are knots in a cloth. Weigh them, and they come out even.

how: Lalla's vakhs are recited and sung in Kashmiri by Hindus and Muslims alike; Kashmiri Shaivism teaches the recognition of Shiva as one's own Self.

o: a Kashmiri queen who built temples across the valley
a Kashmiri yogini of Shiva whose sayings both faiths quote
a goddess of the mountains worshiped in Kashmir

games.q: Lalla's story and sayings: tap the pairs.
p: a knot for each insult and each praise
the true Self of every being

s: the praise cloth came out heavier in the story
they weighed exactly the same: the knots were just knots.
Lalla is honored only by Kashmiri Hindus
Hindus and Muslims in Kashmir both claim her and quote her vakhs.
in a vakh, Lalla says neither jeers nor flowers change her
let them abuse me or worship me with flowers; I stay as I am.

games.q: you get a glowing review at work and a harsh one in the same week. what would Lalla's cloths say?
o: keep the glowing one, forget the harsh one
both are knots in a cloth; neither changes who you are
believe the harsh one; praise is usually flattery
games.why: praise didn't add to her and insults didn't take away. in her Shaiva tradition, the Self underneath is Shiva.

practice: Hold both hands out, palms up. Let one hold the last compliment you got, and the other the last criticism. Feel them both: no heavier, no lighter.
Then lower your hands slowly into your lap, and rest.
